stem: Leaders at a Calgary marketing agency refuse a client's request to bury automatic-renewal fees in tiny print, saying it conflicts with the CMA Code even though no specific law clearly forbids it. Their decision is driven mainly by:
options: a regulatory force
macromarketing
customer experience management
ethical principles
explanation: The agency is acting on moral principles and a code of ethics, not on a legal requirement, so ethics is the driver. A regulatory force would be a law or government rule, and the stem says no law clearly forbids the practice.

stem: Which statement about codes of ethics in marketing is NOT accurate, according to the chapter?
options: Only government agencies issue codes of ethics for marketers
The CMA publishes a Canadian Marketing Code of Ethics and Standards
Many industries and professional associations have codes of ethics
Many companies have their own guidelines and codes of ethics
explanation: The slides note that many companies, industries and professional associations have guidelines and codes of ethics, including the CMA's Canadian Marketing Code of Ethics and Standards. Codes are not limited to government agencies.

stem: A Winnipeg supplement company's new ad is technically legal, but it implies results that the company's own studies do not support. Which statement best applies?
options: The ad is a CSR initiative, because any form of advertising has some effect on society
The ad may be legal yet unethical; codes of ethics like the CMA Code guide conduct beyond the law
The ad is a regulatory environmental force, which the company itself cannot control
Because the ad is legal, it is automatically ethical, so no code of ethics applies
explanation: Laws set the legal minimum, while ethics are the moral principles governing what an individual or group believes is right, so an ad can satisfy the law and still mislead. That gap is why companies, industries and associations such as the CMA publish codes of ethics. The firm's own ad is a controllable decision, not an environmental force.

stem: The Canadian Marketing Code of Ethics and Standards is published by the Chartered Institute of Marketing.
options: True
False
explanation: False. Corrected: the Canadian Marketing Code of Ethics and Standards is published by the Canadian Marketing Association (CMA). The Chartered Institute of Marketing is the UK body whose definition of marketing appears on the slides.

stem: What kinds of organizations engage in marketing?
options: only those that can afford national advertising
very large and established nonprofit organizations
exclusively Fortune 1000 companies
every organization markets
virtually no organizations
explanation: Every organization markets, because each needs people to engage in exchanges with it or to think or behave in a certain way - including non-profits like the Canadian Red Cross and government agencies like the Ministry of Transportation. Marketing is not limited to big advertisers or large companies.

stem: Alberta's transportation ministry runs radio and billboard ads urging drivers to put their phones away while driving. Nothing is sold. Which statement best describes this campaign?
options: It is macromarketing, because a government is doing it
It is not marketing, because no product or money is exchanged
It is marketing an idea, showing that government agencies market too
It is not marketing, because only for-profit firms can market
explanation: Ideas can be marketed, and governments market when they try to get people to think or behave in a certain way, like the chapter's Ministry of Transportation example. A government running a campaign is still one organization's marketing, not macromarketing (the aggregate flow of a nation's goods and services).

stem: Which statement about who markets is NOT correct?
options: Non-profits such as the Canadian Red Cross engage in marketing
Services, such as dental care, can be marketed
Marketing applies only to physical goods sold for profit
Ideas, such as road safety, can be marketed
explanation: Everyone markets: goods, services and ideas, for-profit and non-profit. Limiting marketing to physical goods sold for profit contradicts the chapter's 'Who markets? Everyone' slide.

stem: According to Chapter 1, why is understanding marketing valuable even for students who will never work in a marketing department?
options: Because marketing affects everyone, knowing it makes us better customers, citizens and career planners
Marketing is mainly common sense, so a marketing course offers an easy and useful credit
Marketing affects only consumer-goods firms, which employ most business graduates in Canada
Marketing knowledge is legally required to obtain every Canadian business licence
explanation: The career slide states that marketing affects all individuals, organizations, industries and countries, and that knowing it makes us better customers, more informed citizens and better career planners. 'Common sense' is the misconception the chapter rejects.

stem: A Calgary food bank seeking donors, a city councillor seeking re-election and the Town of Banff promoting winter tourism all run campaigns. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Only Banff is marketing, because tourism is a service that visitors pay money for
All three are marketing, since organizations, individuals and places can all be marketed
Only the food bank is marketing, because charities are the only non-business exception
None of them is marketing, because none of them sells a physical product for profit
explanation: Everyone markets: non-profits, individuals and places as well as firms, and the offering can be a good, service, idea, person or place. Requiring a physical product or a profit motive reflects the narrow view of marketing the chapter corrects.
